spindle.alt: Thirty days of spindle vibration on machining centre CU1. The RMS velocity holds at 2.2 mm/s for nine days, then drifts by 3.1 mm/s over three weeks to reach 5.3 mm/s. It crosses the ISO 10816 limit of 4.5 mm/s on the twenty-sixth day, at 4.53 mm/s, four days before the end of the window. The critical alarm fires, it is acknowledged, and the spindle is pulled on a Saturday instead of failing mid-run.
spindle.caption: Spindle wear, 30 days
spindle.title: What shows before the breakdown
spindle.lede: A spindle does not fail all at once. Its vibration climbs for weeks, and nobody measures it because nobody looks at it.
spindle.p1: Meshvise reads the RMS vibration velocity on the machining centre, keeps it day after day and compares it with the 4.5 mm/s limit of ISO 10816. On the twenty-sixth day the limit is crossed at 4.53 mm/s, the alarm goes out by email with the history of the three preceding weeks, and it is acknowledged.
spindle.p2: The bearing temperature of the same spindle has risen 17 °C in twelve days. Two independent measurements reach the same conclusion, so the spindle is pulled on a Saturday, machine cold, instead of failing mid-run.

air.alt: One week of compressed air flow on the workshop plant. Production climbs to 430 m³/h Monday to Friday, 06:00 to 20:00, but the flow never drops below 255 m³/h at night or over the weekend, while a compressor at rest draws 45 m³/h. Framing a single night shows the compressor cycling around that floor in an empty shop: a permanent leak of 210 m³/h. The air sub-meter confirms it, 24 kW instead of 4.5, so 19.5 kW across the 5,096 non-production hours of the year, which is 13,900 euros a year at 0.14 euro per kWh.
air.caption: Compressed air leak, 7 days
air.act2: Three days, down at the floor
air.night: empty shop, the flow never drops
air.title: The bill nobody reads
air.lede: The compressor runs at night and over the weekend. The shop is empty, production is stopped, and the air flow never drops back to idle.
air.p1: Over a week the picture is unambiguous: five production days, two days of shutdown, and a floor of 255 m³/h running through all seven. A compressor at rest draws 45 m³/h. The remaining 210 m³/h go into the network through fittings nobody can hear.
air.p2: That floor can be weighed at the air sub-meter: 24 kW where idle asks for 4.5. Across the 5,096 non-production hours of the year, at 0.14 euro per kWh, that is 13,900 euros a year. The leak survey is scheduled for a Saturday, network sectioned, and the floor is compared before and after on the same curve.

meter.alt: Thirty minutes of active power on manual mill FU1, a machine with no digital interface, followed by electrical sub-metering. The trace is first drawn in one stroke and one ink: nothing separates the measurements from the repeated value. At 11:42 the last sample arrives, 7.7 kW, and for five minutes the frozen value still passes for good. At 11:47 the point quality turns stale, at 11:50 driver SUBM1 is declared unreachable and the link alarm fires across eight points and four machines. The link returns at 11:53, after eleven dated minutes of gap, and the held value is never counted as a measurement.
meter.window: the frozen value still passes for good
meter.caption: Sub-meter dropout, 30 min
meter.title: A frozen value looks like a normal value
meter.lede: Manual mill FU1 has no digital interface. It is followed by electrical sub-metering, and the sub-meter has gone quiet.
meter.p1: At 11:42 the last value arrives: 7.7 kW. It stays on screen. Nothing blinks, nothing changes colour, and for five minutes a supervision system that only watches the value sees absolutely nothing. That is the window in which you get it wrong.
meter.p2: Meshvise does not only watch the value, it watches its freshness. At 11:47 the point quality turns stale, at 11:50 the driver is declared unreachable and the alarm fires across the eight points of the four manual machines. The eleven minutes of gap are dated and stay minutes of gap: the held value is never counted as a measurement.

threshold.alt: Twenty-one days of daily maximum cutting oil temperature on the workshop chiller. The curve does not change: it swings between 22.37 and 22.95 °C from the first day to the last. What changes is the alarm limit, lowered from 24.0 to 22.5 °C by a signed revision sixteen days before today. At that tighter scale, sixteen of the twenty-two maxima cross 22.5 °C, and eight alarms fire in eleven days, each self-clearing within minutes, only one acknowledged. A rollback revision returns the limit to 24.0 °C with 1.0 °C of hysteresis six days before today, and the journal falls silent while the peaks carry on unchanged.
threshold.alarm_meta: self-cleared in minutes · one acknowledgement only
threshold.caption: Alarm limit set too tight, 21 days
threshold.title: The alarm nobody reads any more
threshold.lede: An alarm that fires almost every day and clears itself within minutes informs nobody. It only teaches people to stop looking.
threshold.p1: The cutting oil chiller has had the same afternoon for three weeks: the daily maximum swings between 22.37 and 22.95 °C, and crosses 22.5 °C sixteen times. What changed is the limit. Someone tightened it from 24.0 to 22.5 °C, and the alarm started firing eight times in eleven days.
threshold.p2: Every limit change is a dated, signed revision. The burst of alarms that followed therefore has a named cause, and the rollback can be written knowing what it undoes: 24.0 °C, one degree of hysteresis. The process itself was never at fault.

engine.fact_title: The fact published on the bus
engine.single: one producer, as many consumers as needed
engine.caption: Thirteen protocols, one engine
engine.alt: Thirteen industrial protocols listed with their transport, as the Bellecombe demonstration fleet uses them: Modbus TCP, Modbus RTU, OPC UA, BACnet over IP, Siemens S7, MQTT, EtherNet/IP, Beckhoff ADS, REST, WebSocket, Webhook, Sparkplug B and MTConnect. They sort into three families by the way they speak: eight polled at the driver's rate, one subscribed to and answering when the value changes, four pushing their values when the device sends. All thirteen converge on a single acquisition engine, all included in the licence, which publishes the same fact message whatever the source protocol: version, identifier, timestamp, quality and value. That single fact serves the live screen, the history and the alarm rule, with none of the three going back to the device. Twenty drivers, ninety-four points.
engine.title: Thirteen protocols, one engine
engine.lede: Thirteen industrial protocols, thirteen ways to connect a device, and a single acquisition engine behind them.
engine.p1: Eight protocols are polled at the rate you choose, one is subscribed to and only receives on change, four push their values when the device decides. That is the distinction that matters when wiring, not the alphabetical list.
engine.p2: Whatever the source protocol, what comes out is the same message: a version, an identifier, a timestamp, a quality, a value. Every protocol is included in the licence; there is no module to buy per PLC brand.

chain.stamp: timestamp taken at the source, never rewritten downstream
chain.no_reask: no consumer goes back to the device
chain.card_title: No fact lost, no timestamp rewritten
chain.card_meta: replayed in publication order, original timestamps
chain.caption: The data chain
chain.alt: The chain a value travels, from the device to the screen. A PLC, a sensor or a meter is read by a driver at its own rate; the driver publishes one fact, once, on the bus, at topic meshvise slash p slash identifier slash value. The timestamp is taken at the source and never rewritten downstream. Three consumers use that same fact: the live screen, subscribed to the bus, the historian, which writes to the database, and the alarm rule, which evaluates it. None of the three goes back to the device. When the bus link is lost, the driver queues its facts on local disk, up to one million, and replays them in publication order with their original timestamps; the historian holds its own separate store for a database outage.
chain.queue_sub: the historian has its own, for a database outage
chain.title: One fact published once, read by three
chain.lede: A value is read once, published once, and served to everyone who needs it. Nobody goes back to the device.
chain.p1: The driver reads at its own rate and publishes a fact on the bus. The screen subscribes to it, the historian writes it to the database, the alarm rule evaluates it. The timestamp is taken at the source and never rewritten downstream, which keeps two records comparable even when they did not travel at the same speed.
chain.p2: When the bus link goes down, the driver queues its facts on local disk, up to one million, and replays them in publication order with their original timestamps. The historian holds its own store for a database outage. Two separate stores, because these are two separate failures.
